cards.statement: Amazon EC2 On-Demand pricing suits short-term workloads with unpredictable compute needs.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances let you pay for compute as you use it, without a long-term commitment. This suits short-lived or irregular workloads.

source.title: Purchasing On-Demand Instances for Amazon EC2

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Spot Instances provide spare compute capacity at a discount to On-Demand prices.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 sells spare capacity as Spot Instances. AWS can reclaim that capacity, so Spot suits workloads that tolerate interruptions.

cards.statement: Convertible Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances support exchanges for different instance types.
cards.explanation: Convertible Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances can be exchanged for another eligible configuration. This provides flexibility when compute requirements change.

source.title: Reserved Instances for Amazon EC2 overview

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances provide an entire physical server for exclusive use.
cards.explanation: An Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance is a billing discount applied to matching instance usage, rather than a physical server reserved for a customer.
cards.misconception: Confusing a Reserved Instance billing discount with a dedicated physical host.

source.title: Reserved Instances for Amazon EC2 overview

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts support bringing eligible software licenses tied to physical servers.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts provide hardware visibility for reusing eligible per-socket or per-core software licenses. The software's license terms still apply.

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Instances share physical host hardware with instances from other AWS accounts.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Instances run on hardware isolated from other AWS accounts. They may share hardware with other instances from the same account.
cards.misconception: Confusing dedicated tenancy with the shared hardware used by default-tenancy instances.

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation includes a discount on the reserved compute capacity.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve capacity, rather than discount it. Eligible Savings Plans or Regional Reserved Instances can provide a separate discount.
cards.misconception: Equating reserved capacity with discounted pricing.

source.title: Reserve compute capacity with EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservations

cards.statement: AWS Organizations can share eligible Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance discounts across member accounts.
cards.explanation: Consolidated billing supports sharing eligible Reserved Instance discounts across accounts in AWS Organizations. Discount sharing lets another account benefit from unused discounts.

cards.statement: AWS Savings Plans base the customer's commitment on a fixed number of Amazon EC2 instances.
cards.explanation: AWS Savings Plans use a spending commitment measured in dollars per hour. The commitment is a usage-spending amount, rather than a fixed instance count.
cards.misconception: Confusing an hourly spending commitment with a commitment to an instance count.

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 includes cross-Region data transfer in its instance compute charges.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 compute usage and cross-Region data transfer have separate pricing. Transferring data between Regions generally incurs data transfer charges.
cards.misconception: Assuming instance compute charges include traffic sent between AWS Regions.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS can revise cross-Region transfer charges and applicable exemptions.

cards.statement: Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access includes data retrieval in its storage charge.
cards.explanation: Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access has data retrieval charges in addition to storage charges. Retrieval costs matter when comparing storage classes.
cards.misconception: Assuming an infrequent-access storage fee also covers retrieving the stored data.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS can revise the charging structure for storage-class retrievals.

cards.statement: Standard internet uploads to Amazon S3 are free of data transfer charges.
cards.explanation: Amazon S3 waives standard data transfer charges for data received from the internet. Storage, requests, and optional transfer acceleration can still incur charges.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS can revise its inbound data transfer pricing policy.

cards.statement: AWS Cost Explorer helps analyze historical spending trends across AWS services.
cards.explanation: AWS Cost Explorer visualizes cost and usage over time. Its graphs and reports help identify spending patterns and investigate cost changes.

source.title: Analyzing your costs and usage with AWS Cost Explorer

cards.statement: The AWS Billing and Cost Management console provides access to downloadable AWS invoices.
cards.explanation: The Bills page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console provides invoices and charge details. Use it to review issued bills.

cards.statement: AWS Budgets can alert you when forecast spending exceeds a configured cost threshold.
cards.explanation: AWS Budgets supports alerts based on forecast costs. A forecast alert can warn you before actual spending reaches the configured threshold.

source.title: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets

cards.statement: Setting an AWS Budgets cost budget creates an enforced spending cap for the account.
cards.explanation: An AWS Budgets cost budget tracks spending rather than imposing a hard spending cap. Costs can exceed its threshold, even when alerts or budget actions are configured.
cards.misconception: Assuming that a budget amount automatically prevents further AWS charges.

source.title: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets

cards.statement: AWS Organizations combines eligible usage across accounts to qualify for volume discounts.
cards.explanation: Consolidated billing combines eligible usage from accounts in AWS Organizations. Aggregated usage can qualify for volume discounts that smaller accounts would miss separately.

cards.statement: AWS Organizations consolidated billing moves member-account resources into the management account.
cards.explanation: Consolidated billing combines payment responsibilities while accounts remain separate. Resources remain in their own accounts with independent access permissions.
cards.misconception: Confusing consolidated payment with merging the organization's accounts and resources.

cards.statement: Activated cost allocation tags help group AWS resource charges by project in billing reports.
cards.explanation: Cost allocation tags organize AWS costs into business categories, such as projects. Activate the relevant tags so their values can appear in cost reports.

source.title: Organizing and tracking costs using AWS cost allocation tags

cards.statement: Customers create the AWS-generated cost allocation tags used in their billing reports.
cards.explanation: Customers create user-defined cost allocation tags. AWS-generated cost allocation tags are created by AWS or an AWS Marketplace software vendor.
cards.misconception: Confusing AWS-generated cost allocation tags with customer-created tags.

source.title: Organizing and tracking costs using AWS cost allocation tags

cards.statement: AWS Cost and Usage Reports provide detailed records of AWS service usage and associated charges.
cards.explanation: AWS Cost and Usage Reports contain detailed cost and usage data. These records support analysis beyond a high-level monthly bill.

source.title: What are AWS Cost and Usage Reports?

cards.statement: AWS Organizations consolidated billing requires member accounts to pay AWS separately for their usage.
cards.explanation: Consolidated billing centralizes payment instead of requiring separate member-account payments. A member account's cost breakdown is informational rather than a separate bill to pay.
cards.misconception: Confusing an account-level cost breakdown with a separate payment obligation.

cards.statement: An AWS Pricing Calculator estimate is a binding quote for the planned AWS workload.
cards.explanation: AWS Pricing Calculator estimates costs from your inputs; it does not provide a binding quote. Actual charges depend on actual usage and applicable pricing.
cards.misconception: Treating a planning estimate as an enforceable price commitment.

cards.statement: An AWS Organizations member account sees other members' costs in AWS Cost Explorer by default.
cards.explanation: By default, member accounts see their own costs in AWS Cost Explorer. The management account can view cost information across the organization.
cards.misconception: Assuming shared billing automatically grants members visibility into each other's costs.

cards.statement: AWS Basic Support includes help with questions about an AWS account and its bill.
cards.explanation: AWS customers can open account and billing support cases with Basic Support. This differs from technical troubleshooting cases, which require an eligible paid support plan.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS can change which support services are included with Basic Support.

cards.statement: AWS Business Support+ includes a designated technical account manager for the customer.
cards.explanation: AWS Enterprise Support includes a designated technical account manager. AWS Business Support+ does not include that designated role.
cards.misconception: Assuming Business Support+ includes the designated account guidance offered by Enterprise Support.
cards.volatilityNote: Support plan names and designated-staff entitlements are subject to change.

cards.statement: AWS Support response-time targets specify when a reported technical issue is fully resolved.
cards.explanation: AWS Support response-time targets concern the initial response to a case. They are not promises to resolve the issue within that time.
cards.misconception: Confusing the target for an initial response with a resolution deadline.

cards.statement: AWS Trusted Advisor identifies opportunities to reduce spending on AWS resources.
cards.explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor includes checks for cost-saving opportunities in your AWS environment. Reviewing its recommendations can help identify inefficient resource use.

cards.statement: AWS Health Dashboard shows AWS service events that can affect your AWS resources.
cards.explanation: AWS Health Dashboard provides visibility into service health events and planned changes affecting your resources. This helps connect AWS events with potential workload impact.

cards.statement: AWS re:Post requires a paid AWS Support plan to read community questions and answers.
cards.explanation: AWS re:Post community resources are available with Basic Support. A paid AWS Support plan is not required to consult community questions and answers.
cards.misconception: Assuming community knowledge is restricted to paid support subscribers.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS can revise access policies for its community and support resources.

cards.statement: AWS Knowledge Center provides personalized status updates for a customer's open support cases.
cards.explanation: AWS Knowledge Center provides answers to common troubleshooting questions. It is a self-service knowledge resource, rather than a system for tracking private support cases.
cards.misconception: Confusing a troubleshooting knowledge library with support case management.

cards.statement: AWS Prescriptive Guidance generates recommendations by scanning resources in your AWS account.
cards.explanation: AWS Prescriptive Guidance provides expert-written guides and implementation patterns. Its guidance is published technical content, rather than findings from account scans.
cards.misconception: Confusing published expert guidance with automated account assessments.

cards.statement: AWS Marketplace provides a catalog for purchasing third-party software for AWS workloads.
cards.explanation: AWS Marketplace is a digital catalog of third-party software, data, and services. It simplifies finding solutions and handling software procurement.

cards.statement: The AWS Partner Network supports participating companies in developing solutions for AWS customers.
cards.explanation: The AWS Partner Network provides participating companies with technical and business resources. These help partners develop offerings and serve AWS customers.

source.title: Become an AWS Partner | AWS Partner Network

cards.statement: AWS Professional Services provides expert assistance for projects that migrate workloads to AWS.
cards.explanation: AWS Professional Services delivers consulting engagements for cloud transformation. Its experts help organizations plan and carry out migration projects.

cards.statement: AWS Trust and Safety is the contact for routine billing questions about AWS service charges.
cards.explanation: The AWS Trust and Safety team handles reports of abuse involving AWS resources. Its reporting role concerns misuse of the platform, rather than routine billing questions.
cards.misconception: Confusing the team for reporting platform abuse with routine billing assistance.

source.title: Content Domain 4: Billing, Pricing, and Support
